Shepherd and Sheep
SHEP-erd and SHEEP
n. phrase
Shepherd: Hebrew rō‘eh, Greek poimēn; sheep: Hebrew tsō’n, Greek probaton. The shepherd-and-sheep metaphor is one of the most extensive in Scripture, running from Psalm 23 and the pastoral imagery of the patriarchs through Ezekiel 34 to John 10 and 1 Peter 5.

📖 Biblical Definition

The shepherd-and-sheep metaphor is one of the most extensive and pastorally rich in Scripture, governing the LORD’s relationship to His people across both testaments. The OT imagery is foundational. Psalm 23: the LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake. The shepherd-psalm is perhaps the most-loved passage in the Bible, condensing the pastoral imagery into its most tender expression. Ezekiel 34 develops the doctrine at length: the LORD’s indictment of the false shepherds of Israel who fed themselves rather than the flock, followed by His promise to seek out His sheep Himself and to set up one shepherd over them, even my servant David (Ezek 34:23)—the prophetic anticipation of the Greater David who would come. Jeremiah 23 makes the same indictment-and-promise: the LORD will raise up a righteous Branch who shall shepherd His people in righteousness. The supreme New Testament use is John 10, Christ’s great I AM-discourse on the Good Shepherd: I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep. But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep. Christ identifies Himself as the prophesied Shepherd of Ezekiel 34 and Jeremiah 23, the Greater David, the One who gives His life for the sheep. The structural features of the doctrine are several. First, the LORD as the Shepherd: His care, His leading, His feeding, His protection, His restoration of the soul, His comfort through the valley of the shadow of death. Second, the sheep as His people: weak, dependent, prone to wandering, requiring constant care, known by name. Third, the false shepherds: the religious leaders who feed themselves rather than the flock, against whom the prophetic literature thunders. Fourth, the Good Shepherd as Christ: who gives His life for the sheep, who knows His sheep by name, whose sheep hear His voice and follow Him, who will gather all His sheep into one fold. Fifth, the under-shepherds of the New Covenant church: Peter’s charge to the elders in 1 Peter 5:1-4 to feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; Neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away. The pastoral office under Christ is one of under-shepherding; the elder is accountable to the Chief Shepherd, exercises His oversight as steward, feeds the flock with the food the Chief Shepherd provides, and answers at the day of His appearing. The shepherd-and-sheep doctrine therefore organizes the entire pastoral theology of the Bible, from the LORD’s care for individual saints (Ps 23) through the church’s present life under under-shepherds (1 Pet 5) to the consummate gathering of all His sheep into the one fold of the Good Shepherd at His appearing.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

(Compound entry.) The shepherd-and-sheep metaphor is one of the most extensive in Scripture, governing the LORD’s pastoral care for His people across both testaments—Psalm 23, Ezekiel 34, Jeremiah 23, supremely John 10 (Christ as the Good Shepherd who gives His life for the sheep), and the apostolic application in 1 Peter 5 (the under-shepherds’ accountability to the Chief Shepherd).

SHEPHERD, n. — 1. A man employed in tending, feeding and guarding sheep. 2. A swain; a rural lover. 3. The pastor of a parish, church, or congregation; a teacher of the gospel, and superintendent of a church or parish.

SHEEP, n. — A well-known domestic animal of the genus Ovis; in scripture, the appointed metaphor for the people of God, gathered by their Shepherd, fed and protected by Him, known by Him by name.

📖 Key Scripture

Psalm 23:1-3 — "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He maketh me to lie down in green pastures: he leadeth me beside the still waters. He restoreth my soul: he leadeth me in the paths of righteousness for his name’s sake."

John 10:11 — "I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep."

Ezekiel 34:23 — "And I will set up one shepherd over them, and he shall feed them, even my servant David; he shall feed them, and he shall be their shepherd."

1 Peter 5:2-4 — "Feed the flock of God which is among you, taking the oversight thereof, not by constraint, but willingly; not for filthy lucre, but of a ready mind; Neither as being lords over God’s heritage, but being ensamples to the flock. And when the chief Shepherd shall appear, ye shall receive a crown of glory that fadeth not away."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The shepherd-and-sheep doctrine is corrupted, on one side, by the false-shepherd patterns Ezekiel 34 indicts (pastors feeding themselves rather than the flock, using the office for personal gain, scattering rather than gathering)—and on the other by the over-clericalism that has so emphasized the under-shepherd’s authority that the Chief Shepherd’s direct relationship with His sheep through the Word is obscured.

expand to see more

The false-shepherd patterns Ezekiel 34 indicts have recurred across every age, including the present. Pastors feed themselves rather than the flock: drawing income, influence, and platform from the office without the corresponding sacrificial care for the sheep. Pastors use the office for personal gain: financial enrichment, celebrity-building, the leveraging of pulpit-authority for non-pastoral purposes. Pastors scatter rather than gather: by harsh authoritarianism that drives the sheep from the fold, by neglect that leaves them wandering, by false teaching that leads them into error rather than to the Chief Shepherd. Ezekiel 34’s indictment is sharp and contemporary; the prophet’s LORD who promises to require my flock at their hand, and cause them to cease from feeding the flock; neither shall the shepherds feed themselves any more (Ezek 34:10) is the same LORD who will hold every under-shepherd accountable at the appearing of the Chief Shepherd. The recovery is the recovery of pastoral office as sacrificial under-shepherding, with the Chief Shepherd’s example and Peter’s explicit instruction (1 Pet 5:2-4) as the controlling standard.

The opposite corruption is over-clericalism that has so emphasized the under-shepherd’s authority that the Chief Shepherd’s direct relationship with His sheep through the Word is obscured. Various traditions have, in various ways, interposed the human shepherd between the sheep and the Chief Shepherd, treating the under-shepherd as the necessary mediator-of-spiritual-things in a way that blocks rather than facilitates the sheep’s direct hearing of the Chief Shepherd’s voice in His Word. Peter’s instruction in 1 Pet 5:3 explicitly forbids the under-shepherds being lords over God’s heritage; they are to be ensamples to the flock, pointing the sheep to the Chief Shepherd, not standing between the sheep and Him. The recovery is the proper balance: real pastoral authority under the Chief Shepherd’s appointment, exercised as servant-leadership, pointing the sheep to the Chief Shepherd whose Word is the food and whose voice is the leading; never the over-clerical interposition that blocks the sheep’s direct access to their Lord; never the under-pastoral abdication that leaves the sheep without the appointed under-shepherding the Lord has provided. Recover both ends, and the shepherd-and-sheep doctrine functions as Scripture means it to function: the Chief Shepherd known and loved by His sheep, the under-shepherds faithfully ministering the Word and care, the flock fed and gathered and led safely toward the day of the Chief Shepherd’s appearing.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew rō‘eh (shepherd) and tsō’n (sheep); Greek poimēn (shepherd) and probaton (sheep); the most extensive pastoral metaphor in Scripture, with the LORD/Christ as Shepherd, the people as sheep, the false-shepherds indicted by Ezekiel 34, the under-shepherds charged by 1 Peter 5, and the Chief Shepherd’s appearing as the eschatological day of reckoning.

Hebrew rō‘eh (H7462, participle) — shepherd; both literal and divine.

Hebrew tsō’n (H6629) — sheep, flock.

Greek poimēn (G4166) — shepherd (the noun behind English pastor).

Greek archipoimēn (G750) — Chief Shepherd (1 Pet 5:4, of Christ).

"The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want—Psalm 23’s tender condensation of the pastoral doctrine in its most-loved expression."

"I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep—Christ’s I AM-claim, identifying Himself as the prophesied Shepherd of Ezekiel 34."

"False-shepherd patterns Ezekiel indicts recur today; over-clerical patterns interpose between sheep and Chief Shepherd; biblical doctrine is sacrificial under-shepherding pointing sheep to the Chief Shepherd whose voice and Word feed them directly."
